sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Spring Boot is the default Java backend framework in virtually every product company, and freshers are expected to bootstrap a REST service on day one. Interviewers test IoC and DI because they reveal whether you understand loose coupling — the single biggest design principle in enterprise Java. Getting Spring annotations and auto-configuration right separates candidates who have built something real from those who have only read tutorials.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **IoC Container** = the Spring ApplicationContext that creates and manages all bean objects for you
- **Dependency Injection** = the container injects collaborators into a class rather than the class creating them with `new`
- **Bean** = any object whose lifecycle is managed by the Spring container
- **@Component and stereotypes** = annotations that tell Spring to register a class as a bean automatically
- **Auto-configuration** = Spring Boot reads the classpath and wires sensible defaults without XML or manual `@Bean` methods
- **Starters** = curated dependency bundles that pull in the right libraries + auto-config for a feature (web, JPA, security…)
- **Actuator** = built-in HTTP endpoints that expose runtime health, metrics, and info
- **Profiles** = named environments (dev/prod) that activate different configuration values

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- `ioc-and-di-basics` — drill: explain IoC in one sentence, distinguish constructor vs field injection, justify which is preferred for testing
- `spring-annotations` — drill: know @Component/@Service/@Repository/@Controller differences, @Bean vs @Component, @Primary vs @Qualifier
- `bean-lifecycle-basics` — drill: singleton vs prototype scope, @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy timing, what happens if you inject prototype into singleton
- `spring-boot-auto-configuration` — drill: what does @SpringBootApplication expand to, how @Conditional works, how to exclude an auto-config
- `spring-boot-starters` — drill: name 5 common starters and what each brings, explain transitive dependency management
- `actuator-basics` — drill: /health vs /info vs /metrics, how to expose/secure endpoints, how to write a custom HealthIndicator
- `profiles-and-properties` — drill: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties trade-offs, how profile-specific yml files override defaults
- `comparisons` — drill: constructor vs field injection for testability, singleton vs prototype for stateless vs stateful beans
- `scenario-based` — drill: diagnose NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, circular dependency error, property not found

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What is IoC? How is it different from DI?" → IoC is the principle (framework controls flow), DI is the mechanism (dependencies are injected)
- "Which injection type do you prefer and why?" → Constructor injection — immutable, testable without Spring, fails fast at startup
- "What does @SpringBootApplication do?" → It's a shortcut for @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan
- "How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?" → Reads META-INF/spring/…AutoConfiguration.imports, applies @Conditional checks to register beans
- "What is the bean scope difference between singleton and prototype?" → Singleton = one shared instance per container; prototype = new instance per injection point

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"Spring Boot uses the IoC container — the ApplicationContext — to manage object creation and wiring. Instead of my class calling `new SomeService()`, I declare a dependency and Spring injects it. This is Dependency Injection, and it makes my code loosely coupled and easy to unit-test because I can swap real dependencies for mocks. I prefer constructor injection because the class is immutable after construction and I can test it without starting the Spring context at all."*
